missions/korean-mission/name: Korean revival and the Korean missionary movement (1907 Pyongyang, Korea as a sending nation)
missions/korean-mission/statusNote: Active: South Korea is one of the world’s largest sending nations, with around 20,000–22,000 long-term missionaries reported by the Korea World Missions Association through the 2010s and 2020s. Church growth at home has plateaued since the 1990s amid scandals, denominational division and secularisation, and Christianity in North Korea survives only underground.
missions/korean-mission/summary: Korean Christianity was unusual from the start: Catholicism was brought home by Korean scholars in 1784 before any foreign priest arrived, and Protestantism spread through Bibles translated in Manchuria by Koreans and Scots before resident missionaries landed in 1885. Adopting the Nevius plan of self-support and Bible study, and set alight by the Pyongyang Great Revival of 1907, the Korean church became strongly self-propagating, sent its own missionaries from 1907, endured Japanese colonial rule, the Shinto shrine crisis, war and division, and after 1970 grew into a global missionary force — while also exporting megachurch, prosperity and highly competitive styles of ministry.
missions/korean-mission/story:
Christianity reached Korea through Korean initiative. Confucian scholars studying Catholic books written in Chinese by Matteo Ricci and other Jesuits sent Yi Seung-hun to Beijing, where he was baptised in 1784; returning home he baptised others, and a lay-led Catholic church existed for a decade before the first priest, the Chinese Zhou Wenmo, arrived in 1795. Refusal of ancestor rites brought fierce persecution in 1801, 1839, 1846 and above all 1866, when perhaps 8,000 Catholics were killed. Protestantism came by a similar route: in Mukden (Shenyang) the Scottish missionary John Ross and Korean helpers translated the Gospels (New Testament 1887), and colporteurs such as Seo Sang-ryun carried them across the border, gathering a believing community at Sorae in Hwanghae before any Protestant missionary resided in Korea.

The American Presbyterian doctor Horace Allen arrived in 1884, and the Presbyterian Horace Underwood and the Methodist Henry Appenzeller landed at Chemulpo (Incheon) at Easter 1885. In 1890 the Presbyterian missionaries invited John Nevius from Shandong, and adopted his plan: Korean believers would support their own pastors and buildings, evangelise their neighbours and study the Bible systematically in winter Bible classes. Missionaries did much — hospitals (Severance), schools (Ewha, Yonsei’s forerunners, Pai Chai), the promotion of the vernacular Hangul script — but the method placed responsibility on Koreans from the beginning.

The Great Revival broke out at the Jangdaehyun (Central) Church in Pyongyang during the winter Bible class of January 1907. After elder Gil Seon-ju and others publicly confessed sins, waves of weeping, confession and reconciliation spread through the city and across the peninsula; the practices of daybreak prayer (saebyeok gido) and unison audible prayer (tongseong gido) that still mark Korean Protestantism date from this era. The same year the first seven Korean Presbyterian ministers were ordained and the new presbytery sent Yi Ki-pung as missionary to Jeju Island; in 1912 the General Assembly was organised, and in 1913 it sent three Korean missionaries to Laiyang in Shandong, China. Koreans also followed emigrants to Japan, Manchuria, Siberia, Hawaii and California.

Under Japanese rule (1910–45) Christianity became tied to Korean national identity. Sixteen of the thirty-three signatories of the 1919 March First independence declaration were Christians, and churches suffered reprisals such as the Jeam-ri massacre. In the 1930s the authorities demanded worship at Shinto shrines; in 1938 the Presbyterian General Assembly, under police pressure, declared shrine worship a civic act, while resisters such as the pastor Ju Gi-cheol died in prison (1944). After liberation, quarrels over this compromise split the Presbyterians (the Koshin church, 1952), and further divisions followed over biblical criticism (Kijang, 1953) and membership of the World Council of Churches (Tonghap and Hapdong, 1959). The communist north, where Pyongyang had been called the ‘Jerusalem of the East’, drove Christians south or underground.

In the decades of industrialisation after the Korean War the churches grew dramatically: Protestants rose from a few hundred thousand in 1950 to about 6.5 million in the 1985 census and about 9.7 million (19.7%) in 2015, with Catholics another 3.9 million. Mass rallies (Billy Graham’s Seoul crusade of 1973, Explo ’74) and cell-group megachurches such as David Yonggi Cho’s Yoido Full Gospel Church, founded in a tent in 1958 with Choi Ja-sil and later claiming over 700,000 members, made Seoul a showcase of church growth. Cho’s ‘threefold blessing’ (spiritual, physical and material, drawn from 3 John 2) was widely criticised as a prosperity gospel; at the same time minjung theologians such as Ahn Byung-mu and many Christians stood with workers and the democracy movement against military rule.

From the late 1970s Korean missionaries went abroad in rapidly rising numbers — fewer than a hundred in 1979, about 1,600 by 1990, about 8,000 by 2000 and over 20,000 by the 2010s — to China, the Philippines, Japan, Central Asia, Russia, Africa, Latin America and the Muslim world. Korean missions mobilised churches, prayer and short-term teams with remarkable energy, but also met criticism for planting Korean denominational structures abroad, competition between agencies, paternalism toward local churches and risky evangelism, made vivid when twenty-three volunteers from Saemmul Church were kidnapped by the Taliban in Afghanistan in 2007 and two were killed. In 2024 the Fourth Lausanne Congress met at Incheon, symbolising Korea’s place at the centre of global evangelical mission.
missions/korean-mission/beliefs/0: Evangelical Protestant conviction of the Bible’s authority, conversion and the necessity of evangelism, fixed early by missionaries largely of conservative Presbyterian and Methodist outlook.
missions/korean-mission/beliefs/1: Fervent, disciplined prayer — daybreak prayer, all-night prayer, prayer mountains and unison spoken prayer — as the engine of revival.
missions/korean-mission/beliefs/2: Public repentance and moral reform, including abstinence from alcohol and tobacco and the rejection of ancestor rites.
missions/korean-mission/beliefs/3: Strict Sunday observance and tithing as marks of a committed believer.
missions/korean-mission/beliefs/4: A strong sense that Korea, a small and suffering nation, has been called to carry the gospel to the world, often expressed as a debt to the missionaries it received.
missions/korean-mission/beliefs/5: In Pentecostal and charismatic streams, Spirit baptism, healing and Cho’s ‘fivefold gospel and threefold blessing’.
missions/korean-mission/strategies/0: The Nevius plan: self-supporting congregations, Korean-funded pastors and buildings, and evangelism by every believer.
missions/korean-mission/strategies/1: Winter and summer Bible classes and later Bible study cell groups, which trained a literate lay leadership.
missions/korean-mission/strategies/2: Use of the Hangul script for Bibles, hymns and tracts, making literacy and faith spread together.
missions/korean-mission/strategies/3: Institution-building: hospitals, mission schools and universities such as Yonsei and Ewha, which shaped modern Korean elites.
missions/korean-mission/strategies/4: Cell-group (home group) systems and mass rallies that allowed megachurches to grow without losing pastoral oversight.
missions/korean-mission/strategies/5: Denominational and church-based mission sending, short-term teams, diaspora churches and partnership through the Korea World Missions Association (1990).
missions/korean-mission/groupsReached/0: Northern provincial towns and the commercial class of Pyongyang and Pyongan, where Protestantism first became a mass movement.
missions/korean-mission/groupsReached/1: Women, who were reached by ‘Bible women’ and girls’ schools and became the backbone of Korean congregations.
missions/korean-mission/groupsReached/2: Urban migrants and the poor of Seoul during the rapid industrialisation of the 1960s–80s.
missions/korean-mission/groupsReached/3: Korean diaspora communities in Japan, Manchuria, Central Asia (Koryo-saram), the United States and later worldwide.
missions/korean-mission/groupsReached/4: Chinese in Shandong from 1913, and after 1992 many Chinese and ethnic Korean Chinese through often covert work in China.
missions/korean-mission/groupsReached/5: Peoples of the Philippines, Mongolia, Cambodia, Russia, Central Asia, Africa and the Middle East through post-1980 missions.
missions/korean-mission/challenges/0: Persecution of Catholics in 1801–66, Japanese colonial pressure and the shrine-worship crisis of the 1930s.
missions/korean-mission/challenges/1: The partition of Korea and the Korean War (1950–53), which destroyed the northern church and created a refugee church in the south.
missions/korean-mission/challenges/2: Repeated schisms, leaving well over a hundred Presbyterian denominations in South Korea.
missions/korean-mission/challenges/3: Security and legal risks for missionaries in China, Central Asia and the Muslim world, including expulsions, kidnappings and killings.
missions/korean-mission/challenges/4: Declining growth and rising public distrust since the 1990s, with many young people leaving the churches.
missions/korean-mission/challenges/5: Ageing missionaries, burnout and inadequate member care after the rapid growth of the 1990s and 2000s.
missions/korean-mission/harms/0: The 1938 Presbyterian acceptance of Shinto shrine worship and wartime collaboration with the Japanese empire, for which the church later repented.
missions/korean-mission/harms/1: Prosperity and success teaching in some megachurches, which tied faith to material blessing and fuelled a church-growth competition.
missions/korean-mission/harms/2: Financial and leadership scandals, including the 2014 conviction of David Yonggi Cho for breach of trust and hereditary succession of megachurch pulpits (such as Myungsung Church, 2017).
missions/korean-mission/harms/3: Aggressive or culturally insensitive evangelism abroad, including the planting of Korean denominational structures and rivalry between Korean agencies in the same fields.
missions/korean-mission/harms/4: Anti-communist and nationalist politics in parts of the church, including support for authoritarian regimes in the 1960s–70s.
missions/korean-mission/harms/5: Breakaway movements with controversial founders (the Unification Church, Shincheonji and others) that damaged the public reputation of Christianity.
missions/korean-mission/developments/0: One of the clearest early examples of a self-supporting, self-propagating and self-governing church in Asia.
missions/korean-mission/developments/1: Major contributions to modern Korean education, medicine, women’s advancement and Hangul literacy.
missions/korean-mission/developments/2: A vital tradition of prayer — daybreak prayer, prayer mountains, tongseong gido — now practised by Korean churches worldwide.
missions/korean-mission/developments/3: Christian participation in the independence movement (1919) and later in the democracy and labour movements.
missions/korean-mission/developments/4: Korea’s emergence as one of the world’s largest missionary-sending countries, inspiring other Asian churches.
missions/korean-mission/developments/5: Hosting the Fourth Lausanne Congress (Incheon, 2024) and contributing Korean theologians to global debates.
missions/korean-mission/outcome: From a self-evangelised Catholic community and a Bible-translated Protestant church, Korea became both one of Asia’s most Christian societies (about 28% Christian in 2015) and a major sending nation, though its domestic church now faces stagnation and a crisis of public trust.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/0/focu: Baptised in Beijing in 1784; founded a lay Catholic community on his return.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/1/focu: Helped John Ross translate the Gospels in Manchuria and gathered the Sorae congregation.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/1/outc: Remembered as founder of one of the first Protestant congregations in Korea.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/2/orig: London; raised in the United States
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/2/focu: Church planting, Bible translation and founding of what became Yonsei University.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/3/focu: Founded Pai Chai school and Chungdong First Methodist Church; Bible translation.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/3/outc: Drowned in 1902 while travelling to a translators’ meeting.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/4/focu: Leading voice in the 1907 revival and originator of organised daybreak prayer.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/4/outc: One of the first seven Korean ministers; signatory of the 1919 independence declaration.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/5/outc: Died in prison in 1944; honoured as a martyr.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/6/role: Founder of Yoido Full Gospel Church
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/6/focu: Pentecostal preaching, cell groups and the ‘threefold blessing’.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/6/outc: Built one of the world’s largest congregations; convicted of breach of trust in 2014.
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/7/focu: Read the Gospels from the standpoint of the suffering people (minjung).
missions/korean-mission/keyPeople/7/outc: Imprisoned under military rule; shaped Korean and Asian contextual theology.
missions/korean-mission/countries/0/text: Lay-founded Catholic church (1784) and Protestant church (1880s); the Pyongyang revival of 1907 and post-war growth made South Korea a centre of world Christianity.
missions/korean-mission/countries/1/text: John Ross and Korean helpers translated the Bible at Mukden; Korean Christians later followed emigrants into Manchuria.
missions/korean-mission/countries/2/text: The Korean Presbyterian General Assembly sent three missionaries to Laiyang, an early cross-cultural mission from an Asian church.
missions/korean-mission/countries/3/text: Korean Christian students and workers founded churches in Tokyo and among Koreans in Japan from 1906.
missions/korean-mission/countries/4/text: Korean labourers in Hawaii founded churches from 1903, beginning a diaspora church now numbering thousands of congregations.
missions/korean-mission/countries/5/text: Became one of the largest fields of Korean missionaries, focusing on church planting, schools and theological training.
missions/korean-mission/countries/6/text: After the Soviet collapse Korean missionaries worked among the ethnic Korean Koryo-saram and other peoples of Russia, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
missions/korean-mission/countries/7/text: The kidnapping of twenty-three Saemmul Church volunteers by the Taliban prompted a national debate about the risks and ethics of short-term mission.
missions/korean-mission/journeys/0/title: Seo Sang-ryun carries the Ross Gospels from Manchuria into Korea
missions/korean-mission/journeys/0/peopl: Seo Sang-ryun and other Korean colporteurs
missions/korean-mission/journeys/0/text: Korean helpers of John Ross smuggled newly printed Hangul Gospels across the Yalu and gathered believers at Uiju and Sorae, so that when Underwood arrived there were already Koreans asking for baptism.
missions/korean-mission/journeys/1/title: Underwood and Appenzeller sail to Korea
missions/korean-mission/journeys/1/peopl: Horace G. Underwood, Henry and Ella Appenzeller
missions/korean-mission/journeys/1/text: The two missionaries landed together at Chemulpo on Easter Sunday, 5 April 1885, after preparing in Japan, where the Korean convert Yi Su-jeong had translated Mark’s Gospel.
missions/korean-mission/journeys/2/peopl: Pak Tae-ro, Sa Byeong-sun and Kim Yeong-hun
missions/korean-mission/journeys/2/text: Sent by the new General Assembly as its first foreign mission, the Korean missionaries worked in Laiyang county alongside American Presbyterians; the mission continued until the Communist victory of 1949.
missions/korean-mission/relations/0/text: Korea’s post-1980 sending movement became the model and catalyst for many Asian and other majority-world missions.
missions/korean-mission/relations/1/text: Korean churches were prominent in Lausanne gatherings and hosted the Fourth Lausanne Congress at Incheon in 2024.
missions/korean-mission/relations/2/text: Korean megachurches, especially Yoido, were studied as showcases of church growth and cell-group methods.
missions/korean-mission/agreements/0/tex: Embodied the three-self ideal of Venn and Anderson through the Nevius plan, adopted in 1890.
missions/korean-mission/agreements/1/tex: Shared the evangelical, Bible-centred and conversion-focused piety of the faith missions, as well as the CIM’s stress on prayer.
missions/korean-mission/agreements/2/tex: Embraced the Lausanne priority of evangelism and the unreached-peoples strategy of the 1980s–90s.
missions/korean-mission/disagreements/0/: Conflict over membership of the World Council of Churches split the Presbyterian Church of Korea in 1959 into the ecumenical Tonghap and the conservative Hapdong.
missions/korean-mission/disagreements/1/: Early Korean Catholics, following Rome’s ruling against the Chinese Rites, rejected ancestor rites that Ricci’s followers had tolerated — the issue that provoked the persecutions.
missions/korean-mission/disagreements/2/: Korean missionaries in China have often worked with unregistered house churches, causing friction with the Three-Self churches and Chinese authorities.
missions/korean-mission/deviations/0: The acceptance of Shinto shrine worship in 1938 departed from the church’s own confessional commitments, as Korean Presbyterians later acknowledged.
missions/korean-mission/deviations/1: Prosperity and success teaching in some megachurches moved away from the revival’s original stress on repentance and suffering.
missions/korean-mission/deviations/2: Competitive church growth and hereditary succession of pulpits contradicted the self-giving ethos of the early Korean church.
missions/korean-mission/deviations/3: New religious movements born in Korean Protestant milieus, such as the Unification Church and Shincheonji, departed from orthodox Christology altogether.
